pages.x: France had ruled Algeria since 1830, and counted it not as a colony but as part of France. About a million settlers of European descent, the pieds-noirs, lived there, while nine million Muslim Algerians had few rights. In May 1945 a protest at Sétif turned into a rising, and the French repression killed thousands.

On 1 November 1954 a new National Liberation Front, the FLN, set off bombs and attacks across Algeria. "Algeria is France," declared the interior minister, François Mitterrand, and France sent in the army: by 1956 over 400,000 French soldiers were in Algeria.

In 1956 the FLN carried its war into Algiers, planting bombs in cafés crowded with young Europeans. In January 1957 General Massu's paratroopers were given full power in the city. Within months they had broken the FLN's network in the Casbah, by the systematic use of torture, and thousands of suspects disappeared.

Reports of torture shocked France. Maurice Audin, a young mathematician arrested in Algiers in 1957, was never seen again; in 2018 France admitted that he had died at the hands of a system of torture. The FLN, for its part, killed many Algerians who would not back it, as well as European civilians.

In May 1958 settlers and army officers in Algiers, afraid that Paris would make peace, seized power in the city and threatened to drop paratroopers on Paris. The Fourth Republic collapsed, and Charles de Gaulle came back to power. In Algiers he told the crowd, "I have understood you." Each side heard what it wanted.

De Gaulle's army came close to crushing the rebels inside Algeria, while electrified fences sealed its borders. But he came to believe that France could not hold Algeria by force, and in 1959 he offered Algerians the right to choose their future. In April 1961 four generals tried a coup in Algiers, which collapsed within days.

The war reached France itself. When tens of thousands of Algerians marched peacefully in Paris against a curfew, the police attacked them, and some were thrown into the Seine. The official toll was three dead, but historians believe that many dozens, perhaps far more, were killed.

The OAS, settlers and soldiers sworn to keep Algeria French, waged a campaign of bombings and murders. Still, on 18 March 1962 France and the FLN signed a peace at Évian, and in July Algerians voted for independence almost unanimously. About 800,000 pieds-noirs fled to France within months.

On 5 July 1962, exactly 132 years after the French had taken Algiers, Algeria became independent. Ahmed Ben Bella, one of the FLN's founders, who had spent most of the war in French prisons, became its first leader. Many harkis, Algerians who had fought for France, were left behind and killed in revenge.

Hundreds of thousands of Algerians died; Algeria counts a million and a half. The war brought down a French republic, sent a million people across the Mediterranean, and left wounds over torture and the harkis that France has only begun to face. In Algeria 5 July is a national holiday.
pts: France called Algeria part of France
The war brought de Gaulle back to power
